prerequisites: Complete courses 1.1–1.4: both domain controllers healthy and replicating, DNS (course 1.2) and the domain time design (course 1.3) in place, and course 1.4's sealed baseline — the DISA GPO package hashed in C:\Staging\DISA, the raw results, three checklists and findings record under C:\Evidence\baseline, and handoff.txt with the versions to reuse.

Work at each domain controller's VM console with an authorized Domain Admin account: until course 1.8 builds AdminJumpBox01, that is where administration happens, with SCC on both controllers and STIG Viewer on SBD-DC01.
Leave SCC, STIG Viewer and the benchmark at the versions course 1.4 recorded until this course's rescan is filed.
labNote: This course builds the organizational unit (OU) structure, learns how Group Policy decides what applies, imports the Defense Information Systems Agency (DISA) Security Technical Implementation Guide (STIG) Group Policy objects (GPOs) that course 1.4 staged, and proves the result with a rescan against course 1.4's baseline. Names, paths and versions below are examples — adapt them, but rescan with exactly the SCC version, benchmark release and profile in handoff.txt. Expect STIG settings to change behavior: that is the point, and the reason everything is scanned and recorded.

Microsoft · User Group Policy needs Read permission for computers
Microsoft · Create and manage the Group Policy Central Store
Microsoft · Group Policy Modeling and Group Policy Results

DISA · STIG Group Policy Objects package
DISA · SCAP content and the SCAP Compliance Checker (SCC)

lessons.title: Design and build the OU structure
lessons.summary: Organizational units exist for delegation and Group Policy targeting, not to mirror an org chart. Build the structure the hardening policies will hang on before importing any of them.
objectives: Design an OU structure around delegation and Group Policy targeting.
Create protected OUs and redirect the default Computers and Users containers.
Explain why the built-in Domain Controllers OU stays untouched.
steps: Design the structure by administration: a top-level SBD OU containing Servers, Workstations, Users, Groups, and an Admin OU for privileged accounts. The built-in Domain Controllers OU stays where it is and keeps its name.
Create the planned OUs with accidental-deletion protection enabled. Record each OU's purpose and who will administer its contents; an OU with no delegation or policy purpose is clutter.

Redirect the default containers with redircmp and redirusr: new computer accounts to the Workstations OU and new user accounts to the Users OU. Group Policy cannot be linked to the default containers, so anything landing there would get only domain-level policy, never the OU-linked hardening. Join servers straight into the Servers OU with Add-Computer -OUPath, so they never pass through the workstation policies.

Keep privileged accounts and systems separate: the Admin OU holds the identities that administer the domain controllers. The domain-joined PKI servers from course 1.6 and SBD-DHCP01 from course 1.7 join the Servers OU, and course 1.8 adds a Tier 0 Servers OU and the admin seats' sub-OUs. Do not nest deeper than the delegation plan requires.
lessons.command:
New-ADOrganizationalUnit -Name SBD -Path 'DC=sbd,DC=test' -ProtectedFromAccidentalDeletion $true
'Servers', 'Workstations', 'Users', 'Groups', 'Admin' | ForEach-Object { New-ADOrganizationalUnit -Name $_ -Path 'OU=SBD,DC=sbd,DC=test' -ProtectedFromAccidentalDeletion $true }
redircmp 'OU=Workstations,OU=SBD,DC=sbd,DC=test'
redirusr 'OU=Users,OU=SBD,DC=sbd,DC=test'
New-Item -ItemType Directory C:\Evidence\hardened -Force | Out-Null
Get-ADOrganizationalUnit -Filter * -Properties ProtectedFromAccidentalDeletion | Select-Object Name, DistinguishedName, ProtectedFromAccidentalDeletion | Export-Csv C:\Evidence\hardened\ou-design.csv -NoTypeInformation
Get-ADDomain | Select-Object ComputersContainer, UsersContainer
Get-ADDomainController -Filter * | Select-Object Name, ComputerObjectDN
lessons.check: The planned OUs exist with deletion protection, the computer and user redirects point at the Workstations and Users OUs, both controllers are still in the Domain Controllers OU, and each OU has a recorded purpose and administrator.
lessons.evidence: Keep the OU design sheet: each OU's distinguished name, purpose and delegated administrator, the ou-design.csv export in C:\Evidence\hardened, and the redirect commands with their output.

quizzes.question: What should drive the shape of the OU structure?
answers: Group Policy targeting and delegated administration
The company org chart
Alphabetical order of departments
quizzes.explanation: OUs are an administrative tool. Policy and delegation boundaries define them; reporting lines belong in HR systems.

quizzes.question: Why redirect the default Computers container?
answers: It makes domain join faster
Group Policy cannot be linked to the default containers, so new machines would miss the OU-linked hardening
It is required before DNS works
quizzes.explanation: Redirection sends newly joined machines into an OU where policy applies from their first start.

quizzes.question: Where do the two domain controllers live after this lesson?
answers: In the new Servers OU
In the built-in Domain Controllers OU, unchanged
In the Users container
quizzes.explanation: Domain controllers stay in their built-in OU — it is where the DC hardening policies link in lesson 3.

recap: OUs follow administration, not the org chart.
The default containers are redirected so nothing joins unmanaged.
The Domain Controllers OU remains the link point for DC policies.
lessons.next: Lesson 2 explains how Group Policy decides what applies, before you link anything to these OUs.

lessons.title: Learn how Group Policy applies
lessons.summary: Before the DISA settings arrive, learn how a computer decides which Group Policy objects (GPOs) apply and which setting wins. Map the order, build the central store the import will use, and record what both controllers apply today.
objectives: Predict which GPO wins from processing order, link order, inheritance, Enforced and Block Inheritance.
Explain how security filtering, WMI filters and loopback processing change a GPO's reach.
Build the central store and record each controller's starting policy with gpresult.
steps: Know where a GPO lives. Its settings sit in two halves — a container object in Active Directory and a template folder in SYSVOL — and they replicate separately, by directory replication and by DFS Replication. A change made on SBD-DC01 therefore reaches SBD-DC02 in two steps: before you judge a result there, check that the GPO's AD and SYSVOL version numbers agree.

Learn the order. Policy applies local first, then site, domain and OU, parent OU before child, so the GPO linked closest to the computer is applied last and wins a conflict; at one OU, link order 1 is processed last and wins. Different settings add up across GPOs, but a single setting's values generally don't merge: the highest-precedence GPO that configures it wins, so a user-rights list in one GPO replaces another's instead of adding to it.

Treat the two overrides as exceptions. Block Inheritance on an OU stops GPOs linked above it; Enforced on a link makes that GPO win over everything below it and pierces Block Inheritance. Enforced is not a shortcut — it hides a precedence problem instead of solving it — so this network uses neither unless the exception record says why.

Read what narrows a GPO's reach. Security filtering applies it only to accounts with both Read and Apply group policy (Authenticated Users by default), and computers still need Read on GPOs that apply only to users, because user policy is read in the computer's security context; a WMI filter applies it only where its query is true. Loopback processing gives anyone who signs in to a computer the user settings from that computer's GPOs — merge adds them after the user's own, replace uses only the computer's — so use it only where the computer should decide; lesson 3 meets the one place this course needs it.

Know when policy arrives, and build the central store. Members refresh in the background every 90 minutes with a random offset of up to 30, controllers every five minutes, and gpupdate /force reapplies everything at once, though some extensions run only at startup or sign-in. On SBD-DC01, copy C:\Windows\PolicyDefinitions with its en-US folder to \\sbd.test\SYSVOL\sbd.test\Policies\PolicyDefinitions: from then on, every Group Policy editor in the domain uses these templates instead of its local ones.

Record the starting state before anything is imported. On both controllers, save a gpresult report of the Resultant Set of Policy (RSoP), what actually applied: the Default Domain Policy and the Default Domain Controllers Policy should be the only domain GPOs listed. Read the applied and filtered-out lists — the reasons gpresult gives, such as a security denial or a false WMI filter, are how you will troubleshoot the import.
lessons.command:
# Once, on SBD-DC01: create the central store from the controller's own templates
Copy-Item C:\Windows\PolicyDefinitions -Destination \\sbd.test\SYSVOL\sbd.test\Policies\PolicyDefinitions -Recurse
# On SBD-DC01: links in precedence order, and each GPO's AD and SYSVOL versions
Get-GPInheritance -Target 'DC=sbd,DC=test'
Get-GPInheritance -Target 'OU=Domain Controllers,DC=sbd,DC=test'
foreach ($dc in 'SBD-DC01', 'SBD-DC02') { Get-GPO -All -Server $dc | Select-Object @{n='DC';e={$dc}}, DisplayName, GpoStatus, @{n='AD';e={$_.Computer.DSVersion}}, @{n='SYSVOL';e={$_.Computer.SysvolVersion}} }
# On each controller's console; carry SBD-DC02's report to the same folder on SBD-DC01
New-Item -ItemType Directory C:\Evidence\hardened\policy-before -Force | Out-Null
gpresult /r /scope:computer
gpresult /h "C:\Evidence\hardened\policy-before\$env:COMPUTERNAME-gpresult.html" /f
lessons.check: You can list both controllers' GPOs in precedence order and say why each applies, nothing is Enforced or blocked, every GPO's AD and SYSVOL versions agree, the central store holds SBD-DC01's templates, and each controller's starting gpresult report is saved.
lessons.evidence: Keep both starting gpresult reports in C:\Evidence\hardened\policy-before, the inheritance output for the domain and the Domain Controllers OU, the GPO version listing, and a note of the central store's source and date.

model.label: SBD-DC01
model.text: Its service list includes Group Policy and SYSVOL over SMB 445: the path every domain member uses to read the GPOs whose order this lesson explains.

quizzes.question: A GPO linked at the domain and a GPO linked to the Domain Controllers OU configure the same administrative template setting differently, and neither link is Enforced. Which value does a controller end up with?
answers: The domain GPO's, because the domain is the higher level
Whichever GPO was edited last
The Domain Controllers OU GPO's, because it is applied after the domain's
quizzes.explanation: Local, site, domain, then OU: the GPO linked closest to the computer is applied last and wins, unless a link above it is Enforced.

quizzes.question: A setting doesn't take effect on a controller. Why is setting the link to Enforced a poor fix?
answers: It hides the precedence problem instead of explaining it, and makes the next conflict harder to trace
Domain controllers ignore Enforced links
Enforced removes the GPO's security filtering
quizzes.explanation: Enforced makes a GPO win over everything below it and pierces Block Inheritance. Find out why the setting lost — link order, filtering, or a closer GPO — and fix that instead.

quizzes.question: Someone removes Authenticated Users from a user-settings GPO's security filtering and adds a group of users. Now its settings reach none of them. What is missing?
answers: A WMI filter
Read permission for the computers, because user policy is read in the computer's security context
Loopback processing in replace mode
quizzes.explanation: Since security update MS16-072, Windows reads user policy in the computer's context. Give computers Read — through Authenticated Users or Domain Computers — while only the user group keeps Apply group policy.

recap: The closest link applies last and wins; at one OU, link order 1 wins.
Enforced and Block Inheritance are exceptions to record, not tools to reach for.
gpresult shows what actually applied, and why the rest was filtered out.
lessons.next: Lesson 3 imports the DISA policies course 1.4 staged and links them where they belong.

lessons.title: Import and link the DISA GPOs
lessons.summary: Group Policy is how the STIG becomes configuration. Import the package course 1.4 staged, link each policy where its systems live so the findings marked fix by GPO can close, and keep the lab's deliberate deviations written down rather than silently skipped.
objectives: Verify the staged package and add its templates to the central store.
Import DISA's policies and link them by OU, with account policies at the domain root.
Handle lab-specific deviations with documentation instead of silent edits.
steps: Start from course 1.4's handoff. Read the package release in C:\Evidence\baseline\findings\handoff.txt, confirm the package in C:\Staging\DISA still matches its connected-side hash, and only then extract it. Copy its ADMX files and their en-US ADML files into the central store from lesson 2, without replacing a newer Microsoft template with an older copy of the same file.

Import each policy this network uses into a new GPO with the GPMC Import Settings wizard or Import-GPO: the Windows Server domain controller, member server and user policies, and the Windows client policies for your fleet's release, which stay unlinked until courses 1.8 and 1.13 link them. Keep DISA's names behind an SBD prefix so the source release stays identifiable. An import replaces every setting in the target GPO and brings no links, security filtering or WMI filter. Where the package's user-rights settings name placeholder groups such as ADD YOUR DOMAIN ADMINS, map them to sbd.test's real groups with a migration table — check the package's support files for one before building your own in GPMC's Migration Table Editor.

Link by OU. Link the domain controller policy to the Domain Controllers OU at link order 1, above the Default Domain Controllers Policy, and the member-server policy to the Servers OU, so the systems later courses build there are hardened from first boot. Domain controllers read password, lockout and Kerberos policy only from GPOs linked at the domain root: if the package carries account policies, set those values in a GPO linked there above the Default Domain Policy, because at an OU they do nothing for domain accounts. Use neither Enforced nor Block Inheritance.

Apply the user policy where people sign in. Its settings belong to every session on a hardened server, whoever signs in — an administrator from the Admin OU, or the built-in Administrator in the default Users container, where no GPO can link. So link the DISA user policy to the Domain Controllers and Servers OUs and, in a small GPO linked to both, enable Configure user Group Policy loopback processing mode set to Merge. Record that decision: it is the only loopback this course uses.

Walk the settings that need a decision in this network — anything that assumes infrastructure the lab does not have or conflicts with an earlier design — and record each deviation with its rationale instead of deleting the setting. Check each fix-by-GPO item in course 1.4's findings record against the imported settings, so you know which ones the rescan should show closed. Then, once SBD-DC02 shows the same GPO versions, refresh policy on both controllers and confirm with gpresult that the SBD DISA GPOs apply, that the course 1.3 time design is intact, and that replication still succeeds both ways.
lessons.command:
# On SBD-DC01. True means the package matches the hash recorded on the connected side.
$package = Get-ChildItem C:\Staging\DISA -Filter '*GPO*.zip' | Select-Object -First 1
(Get-FileHash $package.FullName -Algorithm SHA256).Hash -in (Import-Csv C:\Evidence\baseline\transfer\connected-side-hashes.csv).Hash
Expand-Archive $package.FullName -DestinationPath C:\Staging\GPO
# Per policy; take the exact names and folders from the package:
Import-GPO -BackupGpoName '<DISA GPO name>' -TargetName 'SBD <DISA GPO name>' -Path '<package GPOs folder>' -MigrationTable '<migration table>' -CreateIfNeeded
New-GPLink -Name 'SBD <DISA domain controller GPO name>' -Target 'OU=Domain Controllers,DC=sbd,DC=test' -Order 1
Get-GPInheritance -Target 'OU=Domain Controllers,DC=sbd,DC=test'
# On each controller's console; carry SBD-DC02's report to SBD-DC01:
gpupdate /force
gpresult /r /scope:computer
New-Item -ItemType Directory C:\Evidence\hardened\import -Force | Out-Null
gpresult /h "C:\Evidence\hardened\import\$env:COMPUTERNAME-gpresult.html" /f
w32tm /query /source   # SBD-DC01: Local CMOS Clock; SBD-DC02: a domain controller
repadmin /replsummary
lessons.check: The package matched its connected-side hash, the central store serves its templates, placeholder groups map to real ones, the links follow the OU design with the domain controller policy at link order 1 and nothing Enforced or blocked, gpresult on both controllers lists the SBD DISA GPOs as applied, time and replication are unchanged, and every deviation has a written reason and owner.
lessons.evidence: Keep the import record — package release and hash check, each GPO's name and source, the migration table, the links with their order, the loopback decision, and both gpresult reports in C:\Evidence\hardened\import — and the deviation list with rationale and owner.

model.label: Sign in, step 4
model.text: After sign-in, members read Group Policy over LDAP and SMB from SYSVOL. That is how the GPOs you link reach every machine.

quizzes.question: Why does the OU work from lesson 1 matter here?
answers: GPOs link to OUs, so the structure decides which systems receive which hardening
OUs make the GPO files smaller
DISA requires an OU named DISA
quizzes.explanation: Policy targeting is the OU structure's whole job: domain-controller policies to the Domain Controllers OU, server policies to the Servers OU.

quizzes.question: Where do the ADMX templates go so every domain controller's editor agrees?
answers: Each administrator's desktop
The Group Policy central store in SYSVOL
The offline root CA
quizzes.explanation: The central store replicates with SYSVOL, so every Group Policy editor in the domain reads the same definitions.

quizzes.question: A STIG setting assumes infrastructure the lab doesn't have. What is the right move?
answers: Delete the setting from the GPO quietly
Mark the whole package not applicable
Record a deviation with rationale and keep it visible for the assessment
quizzes.explanation: Documented deviations keep the hardening honest. A silent edit hides a decision an assessor will later need to see.

recap: The central store keeps policy definitions consistent across controllers.
Links follow the OU design; account policies live at the domain root.
Deviations are documented decisions, not deletions.
lessons.next: Lesson 4 rescans with course 1.4's versions to prove what the policies changed.

lessons.title: Rescan, reconcile, and record
lessons.summary: The second scan is the verdict. Rescan with exactly the versions course 1.4 used, compare each controller with its own baseline, update copies of the course 1.4 checklists, and give every remaining open item an answer.
objectives: Rescan with course 1.4's SCC version, benchmark release and profile, and compare against the baseline.
Update copies of the course 1.4 checklists and re-answer what the policies changed.
Close or classify every item in the findings record.
steps: Check that the baseline is untouched: the hash of C:\Evidence\baseline-manifest.csv must match the one course 1.4 recorded, and every file in C:\Evidence\baseline must still match the manifest. Read handoff.txt, confirm SCC and the benchmark on each controller are still those versions, and rescan both controllers locally with the same profile. Changing anything between scans makes the comparison meaningless.

Copy each new session into C:\Evidence\hardened\<host name> and hash it, and carry SBD-DC02's set to SBD-DC01 as in course 1.4. Compare each controller with its own baseline: which rules moved from open to pass, which stayed open, and whether any regressed. Attribute each change to the GPO that caused it — the gpresult report names the winning GPO for every setting.

Copy the three checklists from C:\Evidence\baseline\checklists into C:\Evidence\hardened\checklists and open only the copies in STIG Viewer, so nothing it saves can touch the baseline. Import each controller's new XCCDF results into its copy — with the benchmark and the checklist's STIG release unchanged, the import summary should match course 1.4's — then revisit every manual answer the policies may have changed, sbd.test's included, updating Finding Details and Comments with what you observed and when. Save and hash the copies; the baseline checklists stay exactly as hashed.

Work through the findings record. Every fix-by-GPO item should now be closed; if one isn't, find out why — the GPO didn't apply, a closer GPO won, or the setting needs the domain root or a restart. Work in a copy, C:\Evidence\hardened\findings\findings-record.csv: give each item a Resolution — closed by GPO, deviation (for lesson 5's exception record) or POA&M candidate (Plan of Action and Milestones), with its owner and date — and the Evidence that shows it. Treat any new open item as a finding to fix or classify.
lessons.command:
# On SBD-DC01: the manifest's hash must match course 1.4's record; no Compare-Object output means no baseline file changed
Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 C:\Evidence\baseline-manifest.csv
Compare-Object (Import-Csv C:\Evidence\baseline-manifest.csv).Hash (Get-ChildItem C:\Evidence\baseline -Recurse -File | Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256).Hash
Get-Content C:\Evidence\baseline\findings\handoff.txt   # the SCC version, benchmark release and profile to reuse
# On each controller, after its SCC rescan (adapt the path to SCC's results directory); SBD-DC02 then copies its set to SBD-DC01
$session = Get-ChildItem "$env:USERPROFILE\SCC\Sessions" -Directory | Sort-Object Name | Select-Object -Last 1
Copy-Item $session.FullName -Destination "C:\Evidence\hardened\$env:COMPUTERNAME" -Recurse
Get-ChildItem "C:\Evidence\hardened\$env:COMPUTERNAME" -Recurse -File | Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 | Export-Csv "C:\Evidence\hardened\$env:COMPUTERNAME-hashes.csv" -NoTypeInformation
Copy-Item C:\Evidence\hardened\SBD-DC02, C:\Evidence\hardened\SBD-DC02-hashes.csv -Destination '\\SBD-DC01\C$\Evidence\hardened\' -Recurse   # on SBD-DC02
# On SBD-DC01: verify the copy, then list each changed rule twice, <= its baseline result and => its result now
Compare-Object (Import-Csv C:\Evidence\hardened\SBD-DC02-hashes.csv).Hash (Get-ChildItem C:\Evidence\hardened\SBD-DC02 -Recurse -File | Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256).Hash
function Read-Xccdf($dir) { Get-ChildItem $dir -Recurse -Filter '*XCCDF-Results*.xml' | Select-Xml -XPath "//*[local-name()='rule-result']" | ForEach-Object { [pscustomobject]@{ Rule = $_.Node.idref; Result = $_.Node.result } } }
foreach ($h in 'SBD-DC01', 'SBD-DC02') { Compare-Object (Read-Xccdf "C:\Evidence\baseline\$h") (Read-Xccdf "C:\Evidence\hardened\$h") -Property Rule, Result | Sort-Object Rule | Export-Csv "C:\Evidence\hardened\$h-changes.csv" -NoTypeInformation }
New-Item -ItemType Directory C:\Evidence\hardened\checklists, C:\Evidence\hardened\findings -Force | Out-Null
Copy-Item C:\Evidence\baseline\checklists\*.cklb C:\Evidence\hardened\checklists
Import-Csv C:\Evidence\baseline\findings\findings-record.csv | Select-Object *, Resolution, Evidence | Export-Csv C:\Evidence\hardened\findings\findings-record.csv -NoTypeInformation
Get-ChildItem C:\Evidence\hardened\checklists -Filter *.cklb | Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 | Export-Csv C:\Evidence\hardened\checklists-hashes.csv -NoTypeInformation   # after the STIG Viewer updates
lessons.check: The manifest hash matched and no baseline file changed, both rescans used the SCC version, benchmark release and profile in handoff.txt, each controller's changes are listed and attributed, the checklist copies carry the new results and re-checked answers while the baseline copies keep their hashes, and every findings-record item has a resolution.
lessons.evidence: Keep both rescan sessions with their hash lists, the two change lists, the updated checklist copies with their hashes, and the findings record with a resolution and evidence for every item, all in C:\Evidence\hardened.

quizzes.question: Why keep the same benchmark and SCC versions for the rescan?
answers: Newer versions cost more
Results are only comparable when the measuring stick didn't change
DISA forbids upgrading mid-quarter
quizzes.explanation: A version change alters which checks exist and how they evaluate, so the before/after comparison would mix causes.

quizzes.question: A check is still open and the lab intends to leave it that way, with a reason. What is that called?
answers: A false positive
A passing result
A documented deviation — and possibly, later, a POA&M entry
quizzes.explanation: An intentional, justified open item is a deviation; one that will be fixed on a plan becomes a POA&M entry in the authorization path.

quizzes.question: What makes a checklist entry for a manual check defensible?
answers: The reviewer's observed evidence and rationale are recorded with it
The box is checked
It was green in the automated scan
quizzes.explanation: A manual answer without recorded evidence is an assertion. The observation is what an assessor can verify.

recap: Copies of the checklists carry the new results; the baseline stays sealed.
Open items end the lesson classified, never mysterious.
lessons.next: The final lesson turns this into a standing practice with an exception record, owners and triggers.

lessons.title: Set the rescan cadence and exception record
lessons.summary: Hardening is a state you maintain, not a step you finish. Close the course with an owned exception record and a backed-up policy state, and decide who rescans, when, and which event forces an early look.
objectives: Consolidate deviations into an owned, dated exception record.
Define the quarterly and event-driven rescan cadence.
Export and back up the applied policy state as evidence.
steps: Consolidate the deviations from lesson 3 and the items lesson 4 resolved as deviations into one exception record, C:\Evidence\exception-record.csv — rule, setting, reason, compensating measure, risk note, owner and review date — and file a dated copy in C:\Evidence\hardened. Course 1.4's example belongs here — the rule expecting the PDC emulator to synchronize with an authorized external time source, which the course 1.3 design answers with a declared, checked clock. It stays a living record outside the sealed folder: later courses add their entries to it, and it travels into the authorization path as part of the Body of Evidence.

Set the standing cadence: review each quarterly DISA release for applicable updates, and rescan after any role addition or significant configuration change — course 1.6's closing scans of the PKI servers are the first change-driven run. When you adopt a new release, scan once with the new content before changing any policy, so the record separates what the content changed from what your policies changed.

Back up every GPO, export the Group Policy reports, and export each link beside the backup: restoring a GPO from backup brings back its settings and permissions, not its links. Together they make the applied policy state recoverable and reviewable without a live console.

Write the handoff a future administrator or assessor would need — where the evidence lives, which versions produced it, and what is intentionally open — and hash C:\Evidence\hardened into C:\Evidence\hardened-manifest.csv. Course 1.8 later moves SCC and STIG Viewer to AdminJumpBox01 and links these policies to the admin seats' OUs; until then the cadence runs at the controllers' consoles.
lessons.command:
# Seed the exception record from the findings resolved as deviations; add lesson 3's deviations and fill in every column
Import-Csv C:\Evidence\hardened\findings\findings-record.csv | Where-Object Resolution -eq 'deviation' | Select-Object Target, GroupId, StigId, Title, Setting, Reason, CompensatingMeasure, RiskNote, Owner, ReviewDate | Export-Csv C:\Evidence\exception-record.csv -NoTypeInformation -NoClobber
Copy-Item C:\Evidence\exception-record.csv "C:\Evidence\hardened\exception-record-$(Get-Date -Format yyyy-MM-dd).csv"   # once it is complete
New-Item -ItemType Directory C:\Evidence\hardened\gpo-backup -Force | Out-Null
Backup-GPO -All -Path C:\Evidence\hardened\gpo-backup -Comment 'Course 1.5 closing state'
Get-GPOReport -All -ReportType Html -Path C:\Evidence\hardened\gpo-report.html
'DC=sbd,DC=test', 'OU=Domain Controllers,DC=sbd,DC=test', 'OU=Servers,OU=SBD,DC=sbd,DC=test' | ForEach-Object { (Get-GPInheritance -Target $_).GpoLinks } | Select-Object Target, Order, DisplayName, Enabled, Enforced | Export-Csv C:\Evidence\hardened\gpo-links.csv -NoTypeInformation
Get-ChildItem C:\Evidence\hardened -Recurse -File | Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 | Export-Csv C:\Evidence\hardened-manifest.csv -NoTypeInformation
Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 C:\Evidence\hardened-manifest.csv
lessons.check: The exception record has owners, compensating measures and review dates, with a dated copy filed, the GPO set is backed up with its links and reports beside it, the evidence folder is sealed in the manifest with its own hash recorded, and the rescan triggers are written where course 1.6 will meet them.
lessons.evidence: Finish the hardening checklist: the living exception record in C:\Evidence and its dated copy, the GPO backup with its link export and report, C:\Evidence\hardened-manifest.csv with its own hash, the cadence, and the named owner of the next review.

model.label: Offline backup facility
model.text: Where course 1.19 carries the recovery set, including a refreshed copy of this course's GPO backup, under media custody.

quizzes.question: What triggers a rescan before the next quarterly cycle?
answers: Only a calendar reminder
A role addition or significant configuration change
Nothing — quarterly is the only trigger
quizzes.explanation: Change is the other trigger. Course 1.6 ends with exactly such a scan of the PKI servers, and so do the build courses after it.

quizzes.question: Why back up the GPO set as part of the evidence?
answers: It makes gpupdate run faster
DISA requires backups inside SYSVOL
The applied policy state becomes recoverable and reviewable, independent of a live console
quizzes.explanation: A backup plus reports lets anyone — including a future you — verify or restore the applied state without trusting memory.

quizzes.question: Where does the exception list end up in the bigger arc?
answers: It is deleted after the course
